title: How I Teach: the effect of pH on the rate of reaction of amylase n-of-amylase/
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino walks through how she teaches a notoriously confusing GCSE biology required practical by breaking it into small chunks. She starts with eight core questions and reviews prerequisite knowledge using Cold Call and mini-whiteboards. She then builds diagrams slowly: enzyme and substrate shapes, the starch and iodine test, the effect of buffers, and finally the full combination of amylase, starch, buffer and iodine. The explanation is deliberately sequenced so that the combined set-up is less cognitively demanding, with causal chains written out for optimal, low and high pH. Only at the end does she describe the practical itself, including controlled variables, a spotting tile and the expected colour at time zero, before students practise exam questions. She also explains when she prefers mini-whiteboards, Cold Call or Turn and Talk.
points: Complex practicals become manageable when prerequisites are retrieved first and the full set-up is built up in small steps.
Sequencing earlier checks of amylase and starch makes the final combined diagram less demanding on working memory.
Writing out each causal chain for pH 7, 2 and high pH makes the reasoning explicit.
She chooses mini-whiteboards when she needs every student's answer, Cold Call for quick recall during explanation, and Turn and Talk when students can reason from known information.
Previewing the practical last, with labelled wells and repeated links back to earlier diagrams, reduces what students must hold in mind.
quotes: The effect of pH on amylase action is a required practical in the AQA GCSE specification. While the individual components are not very tricky, putting them together tends to boggle the mind of many a student.
I do this in this way and at this point so that the combination of amylase, starch, pH buffer and iodine that is described later on is less cognitively demanding.

To aid student understanding of the colour change, I cover up the words amylase and starch and say that the amylase catalyses the breakdown of starch so eventually starch will be broken down to glucose molecules. By covering up these words, we are left with iodine in the beaker, which has a reddish-orange colour. So, once all the starch is broken down by amylase, the iodine will not change colour and the resulting colour remaining in the beaker will be reddish-orange.
I draw a spotting tile (as below) and say that we add a drop of iodine to each well. I also label each well so there is one less bit of information for students to hold in their working memories.

Throughout this teaching sequence, I quiz the students about facts they have learnt previously and link them explicitly to new information. Read this brilliant blog by Matt ben David on when to use Cold Call or MWBs. If I want to check if all students remember or understand something, I use MWBs. If during an explanation, I want all students thinking but want to quickly check recall, I use Cold Call. If it is something that I think students can work out using information they have, I usually do a Turn and Talk followed by Cold Call*.
